LOS ANGELES (CNN) -- A group of anonymous software developers said they will soon start selling a program that will allow iPhone owners to use the hugely popular device on cell phone systems around the world and not just with AT&T. Apple's iPhone is yet to go on sale outside the U.S. Apple's iPhone, released in the United States two months ago, was engineered to operate for the first two years only on the AT&T system through an exclusive arrangement between Apple and AT&T. It has not yet been sold outside of the U.S. Los Angeles software consultant Brett Schulte, who is not affiliated with the developers, demonstrated the software for CNN Friday evening. An iPhone that had the new software appeared to work on the T-Mobile system just seconds after Schulte replaced the AT&T SIM card with a T-Mobile SIM card. "It's completely software hacked," Schulte said. "There's no case opening required. It's not required to do any kind of disassembly." It took Schulte about two minutes to unlock the iPhone. The developers would not give CNN their last names, saying "We don't want to be hounded." The said they would start selling the software, which they haven't yet priced, as soon as their online payment and customer service systems are ready. They're also waiting for more information from their lawyers. Apple spokeswoman Jennifer Bowcock told CNN her company has no comment. AT&T spokesman Mark Siegel said he couldn't speculate on the legality of unlocking the phone, but he added, "When you sign up, you're signing a two-year contract. You're obligated to pay the bill." "When people buy the iPhone it's clear from our materials it's designed to operate exclusively on AT&T," Siegel said. Schulte, however, said it is possible to buy an iPhone without being contractually obligated to AT&T. The developers recently created a Web site -- iPhoneSIMfree.com -- but there is very little information on it and no direct way for anyone to purchase the software. Internet records showed they bought the domain name less than two weeks ago. Two members of the group, who identified themselves only as "John" and "Liu," told CNN in a phone interview that a core group of six people on three continents worked to unlock the iPhone as a hobby. They said they are fans of Apple products who thought the iPhone should be made accessible to people who cannot use AT&T. "I'm not in America and I can't use it," said Liu, who would not reveal the country in which he lives. "It's not fair." Asked if he thought modifying the iPhone was legal, he said "That's a very good question. I truly believe it is." John and Liu said they have not been contacted by either Apple or AT&T, but said that could change the moment their software goes on sale. # Anonymous Developers Release iPhone Unlocking Software, Freeing Device from AT&T

**A group of anonymous software developers has released a program that allows Apple's iPhone to work on cellular networks other than AT&T, potentially disrupting the exclusive carrier arrangement that has defined the device since its launch.**

The software, distributed freely online, enables users to "unlock" their iPhones—removing the technical restrictions that tie the device to AT&T, currently the only authorized carrier for the popular smartphone in the United States.

## How It Works

The unlocking program modifies the iPhone's software to accept SIM cards from other GSM-based carriers, such as T-Mobile in the United States or international providers around the world. For consumers who purchased an iPhone but preferred a different carrier—or who travel abroad frequently—the tool offers newfound flexibility.

"This is about giving people control over hardware they've paid for," said one developer who spoke on condition of anonymity, citing potential legal concerns. "When you buy a device, you should be able to use it how you want."

## A Legal Gray Area

The release raises significant questions about the legality of modifying devices and the enforceability of exclusive carrier agreements. Apple entered into a multi-year exclusivity deal with AT&T, and both companies stand to benefit from keeping customers locked into that arrangement.

Legal experts remain divided on whether unlocking a phone violates any laws, though some point to exemptions in copyright legislation that may protect consumers who modify devices they own.

Neither Apple nor AT&T immediately responded to requests for comment on the software's release.

## Risks for Users

Technology analysts caution that consumers should proceed carefully. Unlocking an iPhone may:

- **Void the manufacturer's warranty**
- **Cause the device to malfunction** after future software updates
- **Potentially "brick" the phone**, rendering it unusable if the process fails

"There's real risk involved," said one industry observer. "Apple could push an update that disables unlocked phones, and users would have little recourse."

## The Broader Battle

The development highlights an ongoing tension between technology companies seeking to control their ecosystems and a community of developers and consumers pushing for openness. The anonymous nature of the group underscores the uncertain legal terrain surrounding such efforts.

As word of the software spreads, all eyes are on how Apple and AT&T will respond—and whether the companies will pursue technical countermeasures, legal action, or both.

For now, the developers say they have no plans to stop.

"The genie is out of the bottle," one said.

---

**September 2007** — Just weeks after a teenager demonstrated a hardware-based method to unlock Apple's iPhone, a collective of software developers has released a program that allows the coveted device to operate on competing GSM networks such as T-Mobile, directly challenging the exclusive partnership between Apple and AT&T.

The software unlock, developed by a group operating under the name iPhone Dev Team, along with contributions from a commercial venture called iPhoneSIMfree, eliminates the need for soldering or physically opening the device—a significant leap from earlier hardware methods.

## A Software Breakthrough

The new approach means that everyday users, rather than just technically skilled hobbyists, could potentially switch carriers.

"This is about giving people the freedom to use the phone they paid for on the network they choose," said one developer associated with the effort, who requested anonymity given the legal uncertainties. "People spent hundreds of dollars on this hardware. They should be able to decide who provides their service."

Members of the Dev Team characterized their work as a matter of consumer rights rather than piracy. "We're not stealing anything," another contributor noted. "We bought these phones outright. Unlocking a device you own has been considered legal, and we believe users deserve options."

## Apple and AT&T Respond

Apple, which launched the iPhone on June 29 exclusively through AT&T in the United States, issued a measured but cautionary statement.

"Apple has discovered that many of the unauthorized iPhone unlocking programs available on the Internet may cause irreparable damage to the iPhone's software," a company spokesperson said. "Apple plans to release the next iPhone software update later this week. Users who make unauthorized modifications to the software on their iPhone violate the iPhone software license agreement and void their warranty."

The statement was widely interpreted as a warning that future software updates could disable modified phones—a concern that quickly spread through online forums.

AT&T, which invested heavily in its multi-year exclusive arrangement with Apple, declined to detail its legal strategy but emphasized the terms of its agreement.

"We have a great relationship with Apple, and customers who want the full iPhone experience should activate service through AT&T," a company representative said. "We're confident in our exclusive partnership and in the value we provide to iPhone customers."

## Legal Gray Area

The unlocking efforts raise thorny legal questions. While U.S. copyright regulators granted an exemption in 2006 permitting consumers to unlock their mobile phones, the commercial sale of unlocking software occupies murkier territory, particularly where it may involve reverse-engineering Apple's proprietary code.

Industry analysts noted that the situation places Apple in a delicate position.

"Every unlocked iPhone is still an iPhone sale, which Apple counts," said one telecommunications analyst. "But the exclusivity deal with AT&T reportedly involves revenue sharing, so Apple has an incentive to keep phones on the AT&T network. It's a genuine tension."

## What Comes Next

The commercial provider iPhoneSIMfree began marketing its solution to resellers, while free alternatives circulated among enthusiast communities. Both camps braced for Apple's anticipated software update, uncertain whether unlocked devices would survive the patch.

For now, the cat-and-mouse contest between Apple and the hacking community appears poised to continue—a dynamic that may define the young device's future as much as any feature Cupertino unveils.

"Apple can update the software," one Dev Team member said. "And we'll keep working. That's just how this goes."

# New Software Promises to Unlock iPhones, But Legal Questions Linger

*Consultants demonstrate workarounds as manufacturers and carriers push back*

In a modest office suite downtown, software consultant Marcus Delgado leaned over his laptop, a tangle of cables connecting it to a row of smartphones on his desk.

"Watch this," he said, running a program that scrolled lines of code across the screen. Within minutes, one of the locked handsets displayed a home screen it wasn't supposed to show—at least not without its original carrier's approval.

Delgado is among a growing community of developers and consultants who specialize in unlocking mobile devices, freeing them from the restrictions that tie a phone to a single wireless provider. For consumers frustrated by carrier lock-ins, expensive roaming fees, or the inability to sell their old devices freely, such software has become an appealing option.

"People buy a phone, they own the hardware, and they think they should be able to use it however they want," Delgado said during the demonstration. "In a lot of cases, the law actually agrees with them."

## The Consumer Case

Advocates argue that unlocking gives users genuine freedom. A traveler landing overseas can slot in a local SIM card rather than pay steep international rates. A buyer of a secondhand phone can activate it on their preferred network. The used-device market, worth billions annually, depends partly on phones that can move easily between carriers.

Under current U.S. rules, consumers generally have the legal right to unlock a phone they've fully paid for. The Unlocking Consumer Choice and Wireless Competition Act, signed in 2014, restored exemptions allowing individuals to unlock their devices.

But the picture grows murkier when third-party software enters the equation, particularly tools that bypass security measures rather than simply request an official unlock.

## Industry Reactions

Reached for comment, a spokesperson for one major device manufacturer struck a cautious tone.

"We support our customers' right to use their devices on the network of their choice once eligibility requirements are met," the spokesperson said. "However, we strongly discourage the use of unauthorized software, which can compromise device security, void warranties, and in some cases violate our terms of service."

A representative for a national wireless carrier echoed those concerns while emphasizing legitimate channels.

"Customers can request an unlock through us directly once their account is in good standing and any device financing is complete," she said. "There's no need for risky third-party tools. Bypassing our systems can expose users to malware or brick their phones entirely."

Both companies stopped short of threatening legal action against individual consultants but noted that distributing tools to circumvent security protections could raise concerns under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

## A Legal Gray Zone

Legal experts describe the landscape as genuinely unsettled.

"There's a meaningful difference between unlocking a phone you own and distributing software designed to defeat technical protection measures," said one intellectual property attorney familiar with such cases. "The first is broadly permitted. The second can still land you in hot water, depending on how the tool works and how it's marketed."

For his part, Delgado insists his work stays on the right side of the line, focusing on devices whose owners are eligible for unlocking and who have exhausted or been denied official options.

"I'm not cracking into anybody's account or stealing service," he said. "I'm helping people use property they legitimately own. If the carriers made the official process faster and easier, half my business would disappear."

## What Consumers Should Know

For now, experts recommend that consumers pursue official unlocking channels first. Most major carriers will unlock eligible devices at no cost, and doing so preserves warranty coverage and avoids security risks.

Those tempted by third-party software should proceed carefully, verifying the tool's legitimacy, understanding the potential to void warranties, and recognizing that not every product advertised online is safe—or legal.

As the used-phone market continues to expand and consumers grow more assertive about their ownership rights, the tension between user freedom and corporate control shows no signs of resolving soon.

"This debate isn't going anywhere," Delgado said, unplugging his devices at the end of the demonstration. "People are only going to care more about what they can do with the things they buy."

---

*This article is intended as general information and does not constitute legal advice. Readers considering unlocking a device should consult their carrier and applicable local laws.*

## Developers Race to Free Apple's Device from Carrier Restrictions

A new software-based method to unlock Apple's iPhone from its exclusive AT&T network arrangement is gaining traction among developers and consumers alike, potentially undermining one of the most closely guarded partnerships in the mobile industry.

When Apple launched the iPhone, it did so through an exclusive multi-year agreement with AT&T (formerly Cingular) in the United States. That arrangement meant customers who wanted the coveted device had no choice but to sign up with a single carrier. Now, a community of independent developers is working to change that equation entirely.

## A Shift from Hardware to Software

Earlier unlocking efforts required physically manipulating the phone's hardware—a delicate and risky process that could easily render the device inoperable. The newest approach relies entirely on software, making it far more accessible to average users.

"The hardware unlock was never going to reach most people," said a developer who identified himself only as **John**. "You needed steady hands, the right tools, and a willingness to potentially destroy an expensive phone. A software solution changes everything because anyone can download and run it."

John explained that the software method works by modifying the phone's baseband—the component responsible for communicating with cellular networks—without opening the device.

"Once you separate the phone from the carrier lock at the software level, you've essentially given users their freedom back," he said. "They can insert any compatible SIM card and use the network of their choosing."

## International Demand Drives Interest

For a developer known as **Liu**, the motivation extends well beyond the United States.

"People forget that the iPhone was announced with only one carrier in one country," Liu noted. "But the demand is global. Everywhere I look, people want this device on their own networks. The exclusivity deal doesn't serve them at all."

Liu argued that the software unlock represents a natural response to artificial restrictions.

"When you buy a phone, you should own it," Liu said. "The lock is a business arrangement between two companies, not a technical necessity. We're simply demonstrating that the restriction is optional."

Liu added that the collaborative, open nature of the developer community accelerated progress significantly. "No single person solved this. It was dozens of people sharing findings, testing theories, and building on each other's work. That's how these barriers fall so quickly."

## Legal and Business Implications

The software unlock raises complicated questions for both Apple and AT&T, whose partnership was reportedly structured around exclusivity and revenue-sharing arrangements. Widespread unlocking could disrupt those financial expectations and complicate the relationship between the two companies.

Legal experts note that the situation exists in something of a gray area. While consumers may have certain rights regarding devices they have purchased, distributing unlocking tools and circumventing technical protections can invite scrutiny under various laws.

Neither John nor Liu appeared deterred by the potential controversy.

"We're not stealing anything," John said. "People paid full price for their phones. The question is whether they get to decide how to use their own property."

## What Comes Next

Both developers expect a cat-and-mouse dynamic to emerge, with Apple potentially releasing software updates that disable unlocking methods, followed by new workarounds from the developer community.

"That back-and-forth is inevitable," Liu said. "Every update might close a door, but the community always finds a window. It's just the nature of this work."

For now, the software unlock stands as a significant challenge to the exclusive carrier model—and a test of how much control manufacturers and carriers can maintain over devices once they are in consumers' hands.
